newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: South Island Maori in final settlement talks.
newsitem.headline: South Island Maori in final settlement talks.

text.p: Senior negotiators of the South Island Ngai Tahu tribe were in intense negotiations with New Zealand Treaty Negotiations Minister Doug Graham on Monday amid indications an agreement on the tribe's historical land claims is close.
A government spokesman said Prime Minister Jim Bolger "had hoped to have it resolved today".
Beehive sources said the settlement talks were on this morning's cabinet agenda.
The Ngai Tahu team, led by chief negotiator Sir Tipene O'Regan, left Graham's office to hold a brief meeting in the Beehive liftwell mid-afternoon before returning to the talks.
The ruling National government is keen to reap the electoral benefits of a settlement before the October 12 election to add to the $170 million settlement of the Waikato Tainui land claims last year.
The Ngai Tahu have also said they are keen to see a settlement before the election.
The Beehive sources said the talks were now concentrating on "the make or break issues" and the timetable was tight if a agreement was to be reached before the election.
National has put a $1 billion cap on all Maori settlements, but tribes including the Tainui and Ngai Tahu have rejected the notion of a cap while continuing to negotiate with the government.

Last week Graham told a meeting in the South Island city of Dunedin that preliminary Crown proposals could see Ngai Tahu receive a 70 percent stake in farmland areas of high conservation value near Lake Wakatipu subject to a perpetual
lease back to the Conservation Department. The Crown had also outlined a preliminary psoition on offshore islands and Lake Ellesmere east of Christchurch.
In June a partial settlment of the Ngai Tahu claim was negotiated with a $10 million payout and the vesting of greenstone resources in the tribe.
